lesson.title: Synapsis and Tetrads: Where Chromosomes Swap Genes
lesson.summary: Synapsis is the precise pairing of homologous chromosomes into tetrads during prophase I, and it is within this paired structure that crossing over occurs and generates new combinations of alleles.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter on meiosis I mentioned synapsis and tetrad formation briefly as part of prophase I, this chapter looks more closely at what is happening and why it matters so much for genetic variation.

After S phase, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. During prophase I of meiosis, each chromosome finds its homologous partner, the chromosome carrying genes for the same traits at the same locations, inherited from the other parent, and the two homologs align with each other, gene for gene, along their entire length. This precise pairing is called synapsis, and it is held together by a protein scaffold called the synaptonemal complex, which zips the two homologs together closely enough for their DNA to interact directly. The resulting four stranded structure, two sister chromatids from each of the two paired homologs, is called a tetrad, or sometimes a bivalent.

While the tetrad is assembled, something remarkable happens: non-sister chromatids, meaning one chromatid from the maternal homolog and one from the paternal homolog, break at corresponding points and rejoin, exchanging the corresponding segments of DNA between them. This is crossing over, and the physical location where it occurs is visible under a microscope as an X shaped structure called a chiasma, plural chiasmata. A chromatid that has undergone crossing over is no longer purely maternal or purely paternal along its length, it carries a new combination of maternal and paternal alleles that did not exist together on either original chromosome.

Crossing over is the deepest source of genetic recombination in sexual reproduction, and it is worth being clear about why. Independent assortment, covered in the meiosis I chapter, shuffles which whole chromosomes end up together in a gamete, but it cannot mix the alleles that sit on a single chromosome, since without crossing over that chromosome would travel as one intact, unchanged block, either entirely maternal or entirely paternal in origin. Crossing over breaks that block up. If a chromosome carries one gene version, allele A at one location and allele b at another, and the homologous chromosome carries the alternative combination, a and B, crossing over between those two locations can produce a recombinant chromatid carrying A and B together, a combination that did not exist on either parental chromosome before meiosis. Multiply this across the many chromosomes and crossover events happening in every round of meiosis, and it becomes clear why full siblings, who inherit chromosomes from the very same two parents, are nonetheless never genetically identical.

Chiasmata do more than mark where DNA was exchanged. They also physically hold the two homologs of a tetrad together through the rest of prophase I and into metaphase I, which is essential for correct chromosome segregation: a tetrad that separates prematurely, before spindle fibers have properly attached, is a common cause of the chromosome segregation errors that produce gametes with the wrong number of chromosomes. In this way, synapsis and crossing over serve two purposes at once, generating new genetic combinations and helping ensure that each homolog ends up correctly sorted when meiosis I proceeds to anaphase.
